claim: Bees are important pollinators of agricultural crops.
source: Bees are important pollinators of agricultural crops, but their populations are at risk when pesticides are used.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the role of bees in agriculture.

claim: Bee populations are at risk when pesticides are used.
source: Bees are important pollinators of agricultural crops, but their populations are at risk when pesticides are used.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific consensus about pesticide impacts on bees.

claim: One of the largest risks bees face is poisoning of floral nectar and pollen by insecticides.
source: One of the largest risks bees face is poisoning of floral nectar and pollen by insecticides.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about pesticide exposure routes.

claim: Studies of bee detection of neonicotinoids have reported contradictory evidence about whether bees can taste these pesticides in sucrose solutions and hence avoid them.
source: Studies of bee detection of neonicotinoids have reported contradictory evidence about whether bees can taste these pesticides in sucrose solutions and hence avoid them.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in the literature that show conflicting results.

claim: Bees did not avoid consuming solutions containing concentrations of imidacloprid, thiamethoxam, clothianidin, or sulfoxaflor spanning six orders of magnitude.
source: Bees did not avoid consuming solutions containing concentrations of imidacloprid, thiamethoxam, clothianidin, or sulfoxaflor spanning six orders of magnitude, even when these solutions contained lethal doses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the feeding assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Bees did not avoid consuming pesticide solutions even when these solutions contained lethal doses.
source: Bees did not avoid consuming solutions containing concentrations of imidacloprid, thiamethoxam, clothianidin, or sulfoxaflor spanning six orders of magnitude, even when these solutions contained lethal doses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the feeding assays and comparison to known LD50 values.

claim: Only extremely high concentrations of the pesticides altered spiking in gustatory neurons through a slight reduction in firing rate or change in the rate of adaptation.
source: Only extremely high concentrations of the pesticides altered spiking in gustatory neurons through a slight reduction in firing rate or change in the rate of adaptation.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Bumblebees cannot detect or avoid field-relevant concentrations of pesticides using information from their mouthparts.
source: These data provide strong evidence that bumblebees cannot detect or avoid field-relevant concentrations of pesticides using information from their mouthparts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from both electrophysiology and behavioral assays.

claim: Bees rarely contact floral nectar with body parts other than their mouthparts.
source: As bees rarely contact floral nectar with other body parts, we predict that they are at high risk of unwittingly consuming pesticides in the nectar of pesticide-treated crops.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of bee foraging behavior and flower morphology.

claim: Bees are at high risk of unwittingly consuming pesticides in the nectar of pesticide-treated crops.
source: As bees rarely contact floral nectar with other body parts, we predict that they are at high risk of unwittingly consuming pesticides in the nectar of pesticide-treated crops.
evidence: This is a prediction based on inference from the experimental data and knowledge of bee foraging behavior.

claim: The most economically valuable pollinators are bees.
source: The most economically valuable pollinators are bees (Calderone, 2012; Garibaldi et al., 2013; Huang and An, 2018), especially domesticated bees that secure crop yield and quality (Meehan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Domesticated bees secure crop yield and quality.
source: The most economically valuable pollinators are bees (Calderone, 2012; Garibaldi et al., 2013; Huang and An, 2018), especially domesticated bees that secure crop yield and quality (Meehan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meehan et al., 2011.

claim: Insecticides are widely used to protect crop yields in agricultural ecosystems.
source: In agricultural ecosystems, however, insecticides are widely used to protect crop yields (Klein et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Klein et al., 2007.

claim: Using insecticides impacts the health and survival of bees, contributing to recent population declines of all bee species.
source: Using insecticides impacts the health and survival of bees, contributing to the recent population declines of all bee species (Goulson et al., 2015; Potts et al., 2016; Van der Sluijs et al., 2013; Vanbergen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Exposure to sublethal concentrations of neonicotinoid pesticides in food impairs foraging behaviour, homing and orientation behaviour, and olfactory learning and memory.
source: Hundreds of studies have shown that exposure to sublethal concentrations of neonicotinoid pesticides (i.e. imidacloprid, IMD, thiamethoxam, TMX, and clothianidin, CLO) in food impairs foraging behaviour, homing and orientation behaviour, and olfactory learning and memory (e.g. Gill et al., 2012; Henry et al., 2012; Parkinson et al., 2022a; Schneider et al., 2012b; Williamson et al., 2014; Wright et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Only a few studies have explicitly tested whether bees can taste and avoid neonicotinoid pesticides in nectar.
source: Only a few have explicitly tested whether bees can taste and avoid neonicotinoid pesticides in nectar (Arce et al., 2018; Kessler et al., 2015; Muth et al., 2020), but the conclusions of these studies are contradictory.
evidence: This is supported by citations to three specific studies.

claim: The conclusions of studies testing whether bees can taste and avoid neonicotinoid pesticides in nectar are contradictory.
source: Only a few have explicitly tested whether bees can taste and avoid neonicotinoid pesticides in nectar (Arce et al., 2018; Kessler et al., 2015; Muth et al., 2020), but the conclusions of these studies are contradictory.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies with conflicting results.

claim: Sulfoxaflor has been proposed as an alternative to neonicotinoids.
source: In addition, other compounds that affect cholinergic signalling in the insect nervous system, such as sulfoxaflor, have been proposed as alternatives to neonicotinoids, but whether or not these compounds can be detected by the bee's sense of taste has not previously been tested.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of pesticide development and regulation.

claim: Whether or not sulfoxaflor can be detected by the bee's sense of taste has not previously been tested.
source: In addition, other compounds that affect cholinergic signalling in the insect nervous system, such as sulfoxaflor, have been proposed as alternatives to neonicotinoids, but whether or not these compounds can be detected by the bee's sense of taste has not previously been tested.
evidence: This is based on review of the literature.

claim: Insects detect non-volatile compounds through activation of GRNs in contact chemosensilla on mouthparts, antennae, and tarsi which express receptor proteins that bind with specific types of ligands.
source: Insects detect non-volatile compounds (i.e. tastants) through activation of GRNs in contact chemosensilla on mouthparts, antennae, and tarsi which express receptor proteins that bind with specific types of ligands (e.g. sugars, non-nutrient 'bitter' compounds, salts, etc.; Wright, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wright, 2016 and represents established knowledge.

claim: When a taste receptor binds with its ligand, this sets off a signal transduction cascade that results in depolarisation of the neuron.
source: When a taste receptor binds with its ligand, this sets off a signal transduction cascade that results in depolarisation of the neuron (Dethier, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dethier, 1976 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Several types of receptors tuned to bitter substances are expressed in a specialized subset of GRNs.
source: For example, several types of receptors tuned to bitter substances are expressed in a specialized subset of GRNs (Weiss et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Weiss et al., 2011.

claim: When bitter-sensing GRNs spike in response to stimulation, feeding reflexes are inhibited.
source: When these GRNs spike in response to stimulation, feeding reflexes are inhibited (French et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to French et al., 2015.

claim: Bitter compound detection is also accomplished by the inactivation of sugar-sensing GRNs.
source: Bitter compound detection is also accomplished by the inactivation of sugar-sensing GRNs (French et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to French et al., 2015.

claim: Stimulation of the mouthpart's galeal sensilla with neonicotinoids in water did not elicit spikes from any GRNs.
source: Previously, we observed that stimulation of the mouthpart's galeal sensilla with neonicotinoids in water did not elicit spikes from any GRNs, nor did we see a reduction in the rate of firing of sugar-sensing GRNs in the sensilla when stimulated with a mixture of sucrose and neonicotinoid compound (Kessler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Kessler et al., 2015).

claim: Stimulation of galeal sensilla with a mixture of sucrose and neonicotinoid compound did not produce a reduction in the rate of firing of sugar-sensing GRNs.
source: Previously, we observed that stimulation of the mouthpart's galeal sensilla with neonicotinoids in water did not elicit spikes from any GRNs, nor did we see a reduction in the rate of firing of sugar-sensing GRNs in the sensilla when stimulated with a mixture of sucrose and neonicotinoid compound (Kessler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Kessler et al., 2015).

claim: When bees were given a choice between sucrose solution and sucrose containing field-relevant doses of IMD and TMX over a 24 hr period, the bees chose the neonicotinoid solution.
source: In a two choice assay, we unexpectedly found that when bees were given a choice between sucrose solution and sucrose containing field-relevant doses of IMD and TMX over a 24 hr period, the bees choose the neonicotinoid solution (Kessler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Kessler et al., 2015).

claim: Neonicotinoid pesticides in water did not elicit spikes in any galeal GRNs including the nutrient/sugar sensing neurons.
source: However, we also failed to find evidence that neonicotinoid pesticides in water elicited spikes in any galeal GRNs including the nutrient/sugar sensing neurons.
evidence: This is based on previous experimental data from the authors.

claim: Free-flying bumblebees preferred specific concentrations of solutions laced with TMX, but only after a period of at least 10 days of feeding on the solutions.
source: They found that free-flying bumblebees preferred specific concentrations of solutions laced with TMX, but only after a period of at least 10 days of feeding on the solutions (Arce et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arce et al., 2018.

claim: Bumblebees (B. impatiens) are neither attracted nor deterred from consuming sugar solutions containing neonicotinoids.
source: Subsequently, however, another study in a different species of bumblebees (B. impatiens) using methods similar to ours reported that bees are neither attracted nor deterred from consuming sugar solutions containing neonicotinoids, consistent with the idea that they cannot detect the pesticides (Muth et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Muth et al., 2020.

claim: In bumblebee galeal sensilla, stimulation with sugars produces coherent spiking in 2 GRNs which burst in response to stimulation with high-value saccharide compounds.
source: For example, in bumblebee galeal sensilla, stimulation with sugars produces coherent spiking in 2 GRNs which burst in response to stimulation with high-value saccharide compounds (Miriyala et al., 2018; Parkinson et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miriyala et al., 2018 and Parkinson et al., 2022b.

claim: Bumblebees highly value the monosaccharide, fructose, and have a GRN tuned to detect it.
source: We recently discovered that bumblebees also highly value the monosaccharide, fructose, and have a GRN tuned to detect it (Parkinson et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Parkinson et al., 2022b.

claim: The labial palps are critical to toxin detection in other insect species.
source: Furthermore, the type of sugar used to stimulate the sensilla could influence whether bees could taste neonicotinoids (Parkinson et al., 2022b). We also know that the labial palps are critical to toxin detection in other insect species (Chapman and Sword, 1993), and could house additional GRNs sensitive to bitter compounds like pesticides.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chapman and Sword, 1993.

claim: Stimulation of galeal sensilla with sucrose or with OSR nectar produced bursts of spikes resulting from the co-activation of two GRNs (Gal1 and Gal2).
source: Stimulation of galeal sensilla with sucrose or with OSR nectar produced bursts of spikes resulting from the co-activation of two GRNs (Gal1 and Gal2), as we found for individual sugars previously (Miriyala et al., 2018; Parkinson et al., 2022b, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and references to previous studies, as well as Figure 1B.

claim: Each labial palp sensillum (LPIII and LPIV) contained two sugar-sensitive GRNs (LPIII 1 and 2, LPIV 1 and 2).
source: Each labial palp sensillum (LPIII and LPIV) contained two sugar-sensitive GRNs (LPIII 1 and 2, LPIV 1 and 2), but these GRNs exhibited tonic firing patterns in response to stimulation instead of bursts of spikes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Labial palp GRNs exhibited tonic firing patterns in response to stimulation instead of bursts of spikes.
source: Each labial palp sensillum (LPIII and LPIV) contained two sugar-sensitive GRNs (LPIII 1 and 2, LPIV 1 and 2), but these GRNs exhibited tonic firing patterns in response to stimulation instead of bursts of spikes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The spiking rates averaged over 1 s stimulation of Gal1 and the labial palp GRNs were unchanged towards sucrose and 10% OSR stimuli.
source: The spiking rates averaged over 1 s stimulation of Gal1 and the labial palp GRNs were unchanged towards the two stimuli, but the average rate of Gal2 and Gal3 when stimulated with sucrose was lower than the rate for stimulation with 10% OSR (Figure 1C, LME, stimulus*GRN F6,1607=9.16, P<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The average rate of Gal2 and Gal3 when stimulated with sucrose was lower than the rate for stimulation with 10% OSR.
source: The spiking rates averaged over 1 s stimulation of Gal1 and the labial palp GRNs were unchanged towards the two stimuli, but the average rate of Gal2 and Gal3 when stimulated with sucrose was lower than the rate for stimulation with 10% OSR (Figure 1C, LME, stimulus*GRN F6,1607=9.16, P<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Gal3 was active only when stimulated with 10% OSR, but not by an equimolar sucrose solution.
source: (Note: Gal3 was active only when stimulated with 10% OSR, but not by an equimolar sucrose solution, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The rate of adaptation of labial palp GRNs was not significantly different for 10% OSR or sucrose.
source: We found that the rate of adaptation, measured by the change in the interspike interval of labial palp GRNs, was not significantly different for 10% OSR or sucrose (Figure 1D, stim: F1,461=3.11, p=0.079; time, F1,450=586, p<0.0001; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Galeal GRN burst structure (Gal1 and Gal2) differed between OSR and sucrose stimuli.
source: However, galeal GRN burst structure (Gal1 and Gal2) differed between stimuli (Figure 1E, stim*GRN: F1,938=13.8, p=0.0002, time: F1,938=1.42, p=0.23).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: OSR elicited a 20% higher burst rate than sucrose.
source: OSR elicited a 20% higher burst rate (i.e. Gal2 rate, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and shorter bursts (i.e. fewer Gal1 spikes per burst, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), although the rate of adaptation of Gal1 did not differ as a function of stimulus (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: OSR elicited shorter bursts (i.e. fewer Gal1 spikes per burst) than sucrose.
source: OSR elicited a 20% higher burst rate (i.e. Gal2 rate, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and shorter bursts (i.e. fewer Gal1 spikes per burst, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), although the rate of adaptation of Gal1 did not differ as a function of stimulus (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The rate of adaptation of Gal1 did not differ as a function of stimulus (OSR vs sucrose).
source: OSR elicited a 20% higher burst rate (i.e. Gal2 rate, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and shorter bursts (i.e. fewer Gal1 spikes per burst, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), although the rate of adaptation of Gal1 did not differ as a function of stimulus (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A clustering algorithm predicted two statistically separate stimulation groups, one for OSR and one for sucrose.
source: To understand if the population of neurons we recorded from contained information about stimulus identity, we combined the temporal responses binned at 100ms intervals over 1 s of recording of all 7 GRNs across mouthparts using a clustering algorithm (t-SNE and k-means clustering). The algorithm predicted two statistically separate stimulation groups, one for OSR and one for sucrose (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis using t-SNE and k-means clustering shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The total volume of the 10% OSR and equimolar sucrose solutions consumed by bumblebees was not significantly different in the free-feeding assay.
source: In spite of the differences observed in GRN responses, the total volume of the 10% OSR and equimolar sucrose solutions (1.79 M, Figure 1G) consumed by bumblebees was not significantly different in the free-feeding assay (Figure 1H, LME, F1,28 = 2.09, p=0.16).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: There was no difference in the duration of the first feeding bout between OSR and sucrose solutions.
source: We also did not observe a difference in the duration of the first feeding bout (Figure 1I, LME, F1,26 = 0.176, p=0.678), or the total time the bees spent in contact with the solutions over 2 min (Figure 1J, LME, LME, F1,26 = 0.555, p=0.463).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: There was no difference in the total time the bees spent in contact with OSR and sucrose solutions over 2 min.
source: We also did not observe a difference in the duration of the first feeding bout (Figure 1I, LME, F1,26 = 0.176, p=0.678), or the total time the bees spent in contact with the solutions over 2 min (Figure 1J, LME, LME, F1,26 = 0.555, p=0.463).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1J.

claim: A greater volume of sucrose was consumed for the 1 M and 1.5 M concentrations than for the OSR solution.
source: We tested whether the concentration of these sugar solutions influenced behaviour using a concentration gradient of OSR and sucrose solutions at 2.0, 1.5, 1.0, 0.5 M and water. A greater volume of sucrose was consumed for the 1 M and 1.5 M concentrations than for the OSR solution, but there was no difference at any other concentration (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A 1 mM QUI concentration suppressed all galeal and labial palp GRNs.
source: A 1 mM QUI concentration suppressed all galeal and labial palp GRNs, while 0.1 mM QUI suppressed the activity of LPIII2 and LPIV2 alone (Figure 2A, LME, stimulus*GRN F12,1581=11.3, p<0.0001, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 0.1 mM QUI suppressed the activity of LPIII2 and LPIV2 alone.
source: A 1 mM QUI concentration suppressed all galeal and labial palp GRNs, while 0.1 mM QUI suppressed the activity of LPIII2 and LPIV2 alone (Figure 2A, LME, stimulus*GRN F12,1581=11.3, p<0.0001, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The rate of adaptation of the labial palp GRNs was faster when they were stimulated with the 0.1 mM QUI solution.
source: The rate of adaptation, however, of the labial palp GRNs was faster when they were stimulated with the 0.1 mM QUI solution (Figure 2B, stim*time: F1,450=13.8, p=0.0002).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Galeal GRN burst structure was affected by the addition of QUI.
source: Galeal GRN burst structure was affected by the addition of QUI (Figure 2C, stim*GRN: F2,1116=308, p<0.0001, time: F1,1116=0.062, p=0.803; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Gal1 adapted faster when stimulated with 0.1 mM QUI compared to OSR, although there was no effect on Gal2.
source: Gal1 adapted faster when stimulated with 0.1 mM QUI compared to QUI, although there was no effect on Gal2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Clustering of all GRN responses predicted two groups, with the responses to 1 mM QUI separating from the responses to 10% OSR and 0.1 mM QUI.
source: Clustering of all GRN responses predicted two groups, with the responses to 1 mM QUI separating from the responses to 10% OSR and 0.1 mM QUI (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis using clustering shown in Figure 2D.

claim: OSR and 0.1 mM QUI GRN responses were not significantly different according to clustering analysis.
source: OSR and 0.1 mM QUI were not significantly different.
evidence: This is supported by clustering analysis of GRN responses.

claim: Bumblebees consumed significantly less OSR solution when it contained 0.1 mM QUI.
source: The detection threshold observed in the behaviour experiments was lower than predicted by the t-SNE clustering but consistent with our measurements of adaptation in labial palp neurons. Bumblebees consumed significantly less OSR solution when it contained 0.1 mM QUI, while 1 mM QUI was completely deterrent (Figure 2E, LME, concentration: F2,35=49.1, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 1 mM QUI was completely deterrent to bumblebees.
source: Bumblebees consumed significantly less OSR solution when it contained 0.1 mM QUI, while 1 mM QUI was completely deterrent (Figure 2E, LME, concentration: F2,35=49.1, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Bees tested with 1 mM QUI exhibited much shorter average first feeding bout duration than those fed with OSR or 0.1 mM QUI solution.
source: However, the structure of feeding towards 1 mM QUI was similar to the results found for the cluster analysis of the GRNs: bees tested with 1 mM QUI exhibited much shorter average first feeding bout duration (Figure 2F, LME, concentration: F2,40=18.2, p<0.0001) and shorter average cumulative bout duration (Figure 2G, LME, concentration: F2,36=61.5, p<0.0001) than those fed with OSR or 0.1 mM QUI solution.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Bees tested with 1 mM QUI exhibited shorter average cumulative bout duration than those fed with OSR or 0.1 mM QUI solution.
source: However, the structure of feeding towards 1 mM QUI was similar to the results found for the cluster analysis of the GRNs: bees tested with 1 mM QUI exhibited much shorter average first feeding bout duration (Figure 2F, LME, concentration: F2,40=18.2, p<0.0001) and shorter average cumulative bout duration (Figure 2G, LME, concentration: F2,36=61.5, p<0.0001) than those fed with OSR or 0.1 mM QUI solution.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Field-relevant concentrations of neonicotinoid pesticides were not detected by galeal GRNs.
source: In our previous work (Kessler et al., 2015), field-relevent concentrations of neonicotinoid pesticides were not detected by galeal GRNs. Here, we used OSR instead of sucrose and included sulfoxaflor. We also extended this experiment to test the labial palps. As before, we found no significant difference in galeal GRN responses between the control (OSR) solution and all of the solutions containing pesticides at field-relevant concentrations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and current experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant differences were detected in the responses of the labial palp neurons to pesticide solutions at field-relevant concentrations.
source: No significant differences were detected in the responses of the labial palp neurons to the pesticide solutions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 0.1 mM concentrations of pesticides are 10–100 k fold greater than has been reported for neonicotinoids from the nectar and pollen of agricultural crops.
source: To test whether all concentrations of pesticides go undetected by bees, we stimulated GRNs with 0.1 mM of each pesticide mixed with 10% OSR. Such concentrations are 10–100 k fold greater than has been reported for neonicotinoids from the nectar and pollen of agricultural crops and are at least 1 k fold greater than the LD50 values for bumblebees (Cresswell et al., 2014; Mundy-Heisz et al., 2022; Siviter et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies reporting field concentrations.

claim: 0.1 mM concentrations of pesticides are at least 1 k fold greater than the LD50 values for bumblebees.
source: To test whether all concentrations of pesticides go undetected by bees, we stimulated GRNs with 0.1 mM of each pesticide mixed with 10% OSR. Such concentrations are 10–100 k fold greater than has been reported for neonicotinoids from the nectar and pollen of agricultural crops and are at least 1 k fold greater than the LD50 values for bumblebees (Cresswell et al., 2014; Mundy-Heisz et al., 2022; Siviter et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies reporting LD50 values.

claim: Sulfoxaflor is present at much higher concentrations in the field (e.g. 71.4 μM) than neonicotinoids.
source: Sulfoxaflor, however, is present at much higher concentrations in the field (e.g. 71.4 μM, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2014.

claim: Stimulation with extremely high concentrations of TMX reduced the average firing rates of LPIII2 and LPIV2.
source: Stimulation with extremely high concentrations of TMX reduced the average firing rates of LPIII2 and LPIV2; none of the other pesticides affected the average GRN firing rates (Figure 3A, LME, stimulus*GRN: F24,2139=1.65, p=0.024.)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: None of the pesticides other than TMX affected the average GRN firing rates at 0.1 mM concentration.
source: Stimulation with extremely high concentrations of TMX reduced the average firing rates of LPIII2 and LPIV2; none of the other pesticides affected the average GRN firing rates (Figure 3A, LME, stimulus*GRN: F24,2139=1.65, p=0.024.)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Labial palp GRNs adapted faster when IMD or TMX were added to 10% OSR.
source: We also examined how the temporal response of galeal and labial palp neurons was influenced by stimulation with extreme concentrations of the pesticides. Labial palp GRNs adapted faster when IMD or TMX were added to 10% OSR (Figure 3B, stim: F1,821=49.9, p<0.0001; time, F1,808=571, p<0.0001), and firing rates of labial palp GRNs over 1 s were significantly reduced (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Firing rates of labial palp GRNs over 1 s were significantly reduced when IMD or TMX were added to 10% OSR.
source: Labial palp GRNs adapted faster when IMD or TMX were added to 10% OSR (Figure 3B, stim: F1,821=49.9, p<0.0001; time, F1,808=571, p<0.0001), and firing rates of labial palp GRNs over 1 s were significantly reduced (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Gal1 and Gal2 spiking and adaptation rates were affected by CLO and IMD.
source: Gal1 and Gal2 spiking and adaptation rates were affected by CLO and IMD (Figure 3C, stim*GRN: F4,1653=3.47, p=0.0078; time, F1,1653=2.33, p=0.127).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Galeal GRN bursting rate was slightly reduced when stimulated with OSR mixed with CLO or IMD.
source: Galeal GRN bursting rate was slightly reduced when stimulated with OSR mixed with CLO or IMD (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), while the burst length was not affected by the addition of pesticides (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The burst length was not affected by the addition of pesticides.
source: Galeal GRN bursting rate was slightly reduced when stimulated with OSR mixed with CLO or IMD (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), while the burst length was not affected by the addition of pesticides (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Clustering using all of the data for each of the sensillum types failed to separate the pesticide responses from responses to the control (10% OSR).
source: We used the same clustering algorithm that was able to differentiate the responses to sucrose and OSR. Clustering using all of the data for each of the sensillum types failed to separate the pesticide responses from responses to the control (10% OSR, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis using clustering shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Field-relevant concentrations of the pesticides in OSR nectar did not deter the bees from feeding.
source: We assessed whether the pesticides were aversive in the range of values that included field-realistic concentrations (0–1000 nM) and one of the extreme values (0.1 mM) added to a 10% OSR solution. Field-relevant concentrations of the pesticides in OSR nectar did not deter the bees from feeding, as the presence of these compounds did not significantly alter the amount of food consumed (LME, concentration: F4,297=0.209, p=0.933), first bout duration (LME, concentration: F4,290=0.648, p=0.629) or cumulative bout duration (LME, concentration: F4,288=0.310, p=0.871) over the 2 min assay period (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: The presence of field-relevant concentrations of pesticides did not significantly alter the amount of food consumed.
source: Field-relevant concentrations of the pesticides in OSR nectar did not deter the bees from feeding, as the presence of these compounds did not significantly alter the amount of food consumed (LME, concentration: F4,297=0.209, p=0.933), first bout duration (LME, concentration: F4,290=0.648, p=0.629) or cumulative bout duration (LME, concentration: F4,288=0.310, p=0.871) over the 2 min assay period (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: The presence of field-relevant concentrations of pesticides did not significantly alter first bout duration.
source: Field-relevant concentrations of the pesticides in OSR nectar did not deter the bees from feeding, as the presence of these compounds did not significantly alter the amount of food consumed (LME, concentration: F4,297=0.209, p=0.933), first bout duration (LME, concentration: F4,290=0.648, p=0.629) or cumulative bout duration (LME, concentration: F4,288=0.310, p=0.871) over the 2 min assay period (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: The presence of field-relevant concentrations of pesticides did not significantly alter cumulative bout duration.
source: Field-relevant concentrations of the pesticides in OSR nectar did not deter the bees from feeding, as the presence of these compounds did not significantly alter the amount of food consumed (LME, concentration: F4,297=0.209, p=0.933), first bout duration (LME, concentration: F4,290=0.648, p=0.629) or cumulative bout duration (LME, concentration: F4,288=0.310, p=0.871) over the 2 min assay period (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: At 0.1 mM concentration, there was no significant difference in the amount of food consumed compared to control.
source: Importantly, we also tested feeding behaviour using an extreme concentration (0.1 mM) of the pesticides in OSR. Even at this very high concentration, we did not observe a significant difference in the amount of food consumed (LME: F4,73=0.872, p=0.485), first bout duration (LME, F4,74=0.392, p=0.814), or cumulative bout duration (LME, F4,74=1.06, p=0.382) over 2 min (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D–F.

claim: At 0.1 mM concentration, there was no significant difference in first bout duration compared to control.
source: Even at this very high concentration, we did not observe a significant difference in the amount of food consumed (LME: F4,73=0.872, p=0.485), first bout duration (LME, F4,74=0.392, p=0.814), or cumulative bout duration (LME, F4,74=1.06, p=0.382) over 2 min (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D–F.

claim: At 0.1 mM concentration, there was no significant difference in cumulative bout duration compared to control.
source: Even at this very high concentration, we did not observe a significant difference in the amount of food consumed (LME: F4,73=0.872, p=0.485), first bout duration (LME, F4,74=0.392, p=0.814), or cumulative bout duration (LME, F4,74=1.06, p=0.382) over 2 min (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D–F.

claim: Bees do not have mechanisms on their mouthparts that enable them to taste neonicotinoids or sulfoxaflor when these compounds are present in nectar.
source: For the first time, we report how populations of GRNs on the bee's mouthparts respond to stimulation with putatively bitter compounds. We verified that bees do not have mechanisms on their mouthparts that enable them to taste neonicotinoids or sulfoxaflor when these compounds are present in nectar.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electrophysiology and behavioral assays.

claim: Neonicotinoids and sulfoxaflor did not change the bursting of sugar-sensing neurons in the galea.
source: Neonicotinoids and sulfoxaflor did not change the bursting of sugar-sensing neurons in the galea, nor did they elicit or inhibit spikes in labial palp neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electrophysiology.

claim: Neonicotinoids and sulfoxaflor did not elicit or inhibit spikes in labial palp neurons.
source: Neonicotinoids and sulfoxaflor did not change the bursting of sugar-sensing neurons in the galea, nor did they elicit or inhibit spikes in labial palp neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electrophysiology.

claim: Bumblebees do not avoid drinking OSR nectar solutions even when very high concentrations of common pesticides are present.
source: Strikingly, we show that bumblebees do not avoid drinking OSR nectar solutions even when very high concentrations of common pesticides are present.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from behavioral assays.

claim: Very high concentrations of pesticides could produce a small but measurable reduction in the spiking of sugar-sensing GRNs.
source: Very high concentrations of these pesticides could produce a small but measurable reduction in the spiking of sugar-sensing GRNs, but these compounds never elicited spikes on their own.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electrophysiology.

claim: Pesticides never elicited spikes on their own.
source: Very high concentrations of these pesticides could produce a small but measurable reduction in the spiking of sugar-sensing GRNs, but these compounds never elicited spikes on their own.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electrophysiology.

claim: Small changes in the rate of spiking caused by pesticides did not translate into features that the clustering algorithm could use to differentiate pesticide laced stimuli from the control OSR solution.
source: What's more, these small changes in the rate of spiking did not translate into features that the clustering algorithm could use to differentiate pesticide laced stimuli from the control OSR solution.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis using clustering algorithms.

claim: The buff-tailed bumblebee's mouthparts do not have mechanisms for the detection and avoidance of common cholinergic pesticides in nectar.
source: From these data, we conclude that the buff-tailed bumblebee's mouthparts do not have mechanisms for the detection and avoidance of common cholinergic pesticides in nectar.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: QUI clearly suppressed the activity of sugar-sensing GRNs in both labial palps and the galea.
source: The known bitter compound, QUI, clearly suppressed the activity of sugar-sensing GRNs in both labial palps and the galea, but it did not measurably alter the burst pattern of firing of the galeal GRNs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electrophysiology.

claim: QUI did not measurably alter the burst pattern of firing of the galeal GRNs.
source: The known bitter compound, QUI, clearly suppressed the activity of sugar-sensing GRNs in both labial palps and the galea, but it did not measurably alter the burst pattern of firing of the galeal GRNs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electrophysiology.

claim: Field-relevant concentrations of pesticides did not significantly alter the pattern or rate of spiking of galeal or labial palp GRNs towards a nectar solution.
source: Importantly, our new data were able to confirm that field-relevant concentrations of pesticides did not significantly alter the pattern or rate of spiking of galeal or labial palp GRNs towards a nectar solution.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electrophysiology.

claim: Small but significant reduction in the responses of both labial palp and galeal neurons was caused by high concentrations (100 µM) of IMD, SFX, and TMX.
source: Although we were able to measure small but significant reduction in the responses of both labial palp and galeal neurons caused by the high concentrations (100 µM) of IMD, SFX, and TMX, this effect was not sufficient for the clustering algorithm to form classes of distinct stimuli for the OSR-pesticide mixtures.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electrophysiology.

claim: The effect of high concentrations (100 µM) of IMD, SFX, and TMX on GRN responses was not sufficient for the clustering algorithm to form classes of distinct stimuli for the OSR-pesticide mixtures.
source: Although we were able to measure small but significant reduction in the responses of both labial palp and galeal neurons caused by the high concentrations (100 µM) of IMD, SFX, and TMX, this effect was not sufficient for the clustering algorithm to form classes of distinct stimuli for the OSR-pesticide mixtures.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis using clustering algorithms.

claim: The output of the clustering algorithm matched the behaviour of the bees for all bitter compounds tested.
source: It is interesting to note that in the case of all bitter compounds tested, the output of the clustering algorithm matched the behaviour of the bees, as the bees did not reject any of the pesticide solutions or the 0.1 mM QUI solution after the first feeding bout.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of clustering analysis results with behavioral data.

claim: Bees did not reject any of the pesticide solutions or the 0.1 mM QUI solution after the first feeding bout.
source: It is interesting to note that in the case of all bitter compounds tested, the output of the clustering algorithm matched the behaviour of the bees, as the bees did not reject any of the pesticide solutions or the 0.1 mM QUI solution after the first feeding bout.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from behavioral assays.

claim: Small differences detected at the sensory periphery do not translate into a sufficient signal across the whole population of gustatory neurons to produce an aversion to foods containing potential toxins.
source: This could indicate that that small differences detected at the sensory periphery do not translate into a sufficient signal across the whole population of gustatory neurons to produce an aversion to foods containing potential toxins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Bumblebees drank less overall of the 0.1 mM QUI solution compared to OSR.
source: Bumblebees did drink less overall of the 0.1 mM QUI solution compared to OSR, however the amount of time they spent in contact with the feeding solution was the same.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from behavioral assays.

claim: The amount of time bumblebees spent in contact with the 0.1 mM QUI feeding solution was the same as for OSR.
source: Bumblebees did drink less overall of the 0.1 mM QUI solution compared to OSR, however the amount of time they spent in contact with the feeding solution was the same.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from behavioral assays.

claim: 0.1 mM QUI is not immediately aversive to bumblebees (i.e. by taste).
source: This suggests that, while 0.1 mM QUI is not immediately aversive to bumblebees (i.e. by taste), they can integrate negative post-ingestive feedback within a 2-min feeding period.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data.

claim: Bumblebees can integrate negative post-ingestive feedback within a 2-min feeding period when consuming 0.1 mM QUI.
source: This suggests that, while 0.1 mM QUI is not immediately aversive to bumblebees (i.e. by taste), they can integrate negative post-ingestive feedback within a 2-min feeding period.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data.

claim: Compounds reach the hemolymph of honeybees within 30 s of ingestion.
source: Compounds reach the hemolymph of honeybees within 30 s of ingestion (Simcock et al., 2018), and quinine causes malaise-like symptoms (Ayestaran et al., 2010; Hurst et al., 2014), so it is feasible that the bumblebees in our behavioural assay factored in post-ingestive feedback while consuming 0.1 mM QUI.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Simcock et al., 2018.

claim: Quinine causes malaise-like symptoms.
source: Compounds reach the hemolymph of honeybees within 30 s of ingestion (Simcock et al., 2018), and quinine causes malaise-like symptoms (Ayestaran et al., 2010; Hurst et al., 2014), so it is feasible that the bumblebees in our behavioural assay factored in post-ingestive feedback while consuming 0.1 mM QUI.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ayestaran et al., 2010 and Hurst et al., 2014.

claim: Post-ingestive feedback did not prevent bumblebees from consuming potentially lethal doses of pesticides.
source: Unfortunately, when fed high concentrations of pesticides, post-ingestive feedback did not prevent bumblebees from consuming potentially lethal doses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from behavioral assays.

claim: The LD50 for TMX in Bombus terrestris is approximately 6 ng/bee.
source: For example, the LD50 for TMX in Bombus terrestris is approximately 6 ng/bee (Siviter et al., 2022), and bumblebees in our assay consumed a median amount of 3.5 ng of TMX when dissolved at 100 uM in OSR.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Siviter et al., 2022.

claim: Bumblebees in the assay consumed a median amount of 3.5 ng of TMX when dissolved at 100 uM in OSR.
source: For example, the LD50 for TMX in Bombus terrestris is approximately 6 ng/bee (Siviter et al., 2022), and bumblebees in our assay consumed a median amount of 3.5 ng of TMX when dissolved at 100 uM in OSR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from behavioral assays.

claim: Gustatory coding is more than the presence or absence of spikes arising from GRNs tuned to detect particular tastants.
source: Our data also indicate that gustatory coding is more than the presence or absence of spikes arising from GRNs tuned to detect particular tastants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: In bumblebees, the pattern of spiking itself conveys information which is a feature that enables the brain to distinguish gustatory stimuli.
source: In bumblebees, it is clear that the pattern of spiking itself conveys information which is a feature that enables the brain to distinguish gustatory stimuli (Parkinson et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Parkinson et al., 2022b.

claim: Encoding of gustatory stimuli is accomplished by the whole population of GRNs on a given body part.
source: This supports the idea that encoding of gustatory stimuli is accomplished by the whole population of GRNs on a given body part (e.g. the proboscis) as was observed in multichannel recordings from the adult hawkmoth maxillary nerve (Reiter et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reiter et al., 2015 and inference from the current data.

claim: Activity across the mouthparts GRN population that includes temporal input over time is likely to be used by the brain to differentiate taste stimuli and to facilitate the valuation of food quality.
source: Thus, activity across the mouthparts GRN population that includes temporal input over time is likely to be used by the brain to differentiate taste stimuli and to facilitate the valuation of food quality.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and previous knowledge.

claim: The changes in the rate of bursting and spiking in the galeal and labial palps were sufficient for the clustering algorithm to classify sucrose and OSR as separate stimuli.
source: Our new data testing the difference between a nectar stimulus composed of a mixture of sugars (OSR) and sucrose clearly illustrates this. The changes in the rate of bursting and spiking in the galeal and labial palps were sufficient for the clustering algorithm to classify sucrose and OSR as separate stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis using clustering algorithms.

claim: Arce et al., 2018 reported that B. terrestris were capable of selectively foraging on 30% w/v sucrose solutions containing TMX.
source: Previously, Arce et al., 2018 reported that B. terrestris were capable of selectively foraging on 30% w/v sucrose solutions containing TMX.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arce et al., 2018.

claim: Honeybees and bumblebees prefer solutions containing TMX.
source: This finding confirmed our previous data that honeybees and bumblebees prefer solutions containing TMX (Kessler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kessler et al., 2015.

claim: Arce et al., 2018 did not observe a preference for or against the solutions containing the neonicotinoids during the initial days of their experiments.
source: Arce et al., 2018 did not observe a preference for or against the solutions containing the neonicotinoids during the initial days of their experiments.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arce et al., 2018.

claim: Individual bees developed a preference for solutions containing TMX if they were confined to feed on a choice between sucrose and sucrose laced with pesticide over a longer time period (i.e. 24 hr).
source: Similarly, in our previous work, we found that individual bees developed a preference for solutions containing TMX if they were confined to feed on a choice between sucrose and sucrose laced with pesticide over longer time period (i.e. 24 hr, Kessler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kessler et al., 2015.

claim: The preference for TMX was caused by the pharmacological action of TMX on cholinergic circuits involved in encoding reward in the insect brain.
source: We concluded that the preference was caused by the pharmacological action of TMX on cholinergic circuits involved in encoding reward in the insect brain (Barnstedt et al., 2016), as we found no electrophysiological evidence to support that bees could taste neonicotinoids (Kessler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barnstedt et al., 2016 and Kessler et al., 2015.

claim: A preference resulting from post-ingestive reinforcement caused by amplification of the brain's response to sugars would be expected to develop following long-term, repeated exposure to a pharmacological compound.
source: This conclusion is consistent with the expectation that a preference resulting from post-ingestive reinforcement caused by amplification of the brain's response to sugars would be expected to develop following long-term, repeated exposure to a pharmacological compound (Palmer et al., 2013; Wright et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Palmer et al., 2013 and Wright et al., 2013.

claim: If TMX caused bees to associate a higher 'reward value' with food found in a particular location, they would learn to return to it in preference over other solutions.
source: If TMX caused bees to associate a higher 'reward value' with food found in a particular location, they would learn to return to it in preference over other solutions.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on knowledge of learning and reward mechanisms.

claim: Gravity feeders do not simulate how bees feed on real flowers.
source: Arce et al., 2018 conducted their experiments using gravity feeders in an enclosed arena, allowing bees to consume solutions ad libitum. Since the feeders did not have visual or olfactory cues, the authors inferred that the bees were capable of tasting the TMX in the solution. However, gravity feeders do not simulate how bees feed on real flowers.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of bee foraging behavior and experimental design.

claim: Gravity feeders have large openings that allow multiple bees to feed simultaneously, enabling them to contact the solution with all body parts, including the tarsi and antennae.
source: These feeders have large openings that allow multiple bees to feed simultaneously, enabling them to contact the solution with all body parts, including the tarsi and antennae.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of experimental apparatus design.

claim: Honeybees have limited bitter detection in sensilla on antennae or tarsi, only observed when the sensilla are contacted with concentrations of compounds like QUI that are >1 mM.
source: While it is possible that the sensilla on the antennae or tarsi could detect TMX, it seems unlikely given that honeybees have limited bitter detection in these locations, only observed when the sensilla are contacted with concentrations of compounds like QUI that are >1 mM (de Brito Sanchez et al., 2005; de Brito Sanchez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to de Brito Sanchez et al., 2005 and de Brito Sanchez et al., 2014.

claim: Field-relevant concentrations of pesticides are between 3–6 orders of magnitude lower in concentration than >1 mM.
source: The field-relevant concentrations of the pesticides we tested are between 3–6 orders of magnitude lower in concentration (see Kessler et al., 2015 for review); such dilute concentrations of a bitter compound present in a highly concentrated sugar solution would be difficult for most organisms to detect.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kessler et al., 2015 for review of field concentrations.

claim: Floral morphology such as corolla length has often co-evolved with particular groups of pollinators with longer mouthparts.
source: Floral morphology such as corolla length has often co-evolved with particular groups of pollinators with longer mouthparts; a long corolla protects nectar when visitors are efficient and reliable pollinators.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of plant-pollinator coevolution.

claim: In many flowers, nectar is hidden deep within the corolla such that the only contact that bumblebees have with it is via the distal end of the proboscis.
source: In many flowers, nectar is hidden deep within the corolla such that the only contact that bumblebees have with it is via the distal end of the proboscis (also the location where most of the sensilla are).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of flower morphology and bee foraging behavior.

claim: In OSR flowers, nectaries are located at a depth of 5–8 mm.
source: For example, in OSR flowers, nectaries are located at a depth of 5–8 mm (Cresswell et al., 2001) and the nectar cannot be contacted otherwise unless the bee bites through the petals.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cresswell et al., 2001.

claim: Bees learn to handle flowers quickly to improve their foraging efficiency.
source: In addition, bees learn to handle flowers quickly to improve their foraging efficiency (Heinrich, 1976) and even extend the proboscis in anticipation of entering the corolla prior to landing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heinrich, 1976.

claim: Bees are unlikely to contact nectar using gustatory sensilla on their antennae or tarsi while foraging.
source: Thus, they are unlikely to contact nectar using gustatory sensilla on their antennae or tarsi while foraging.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of bee foraging behavior and flower morphology.

claim: Nectar palatability is largely determined by the sensilla on the proboscis.
source: For this reason, it is likely that nectar palatability is largely determined by the sensilla on the proboscis.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of bee foraging behavior and sensory physiology.
